questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Personally, it was important to me that the study destination I chose could provide me another aspect to the law and the legal system than what I had been taught at the University of Copenhagen about the Danish/EU legal system. Canada was perfect in this regard, as most of the country follows the common law system. By choosing Toronto, it not gave me another aspect on how the law works in the province of Ontario and Canada, but also how the legal system works in other common law countries. I believe this is a crucial aspect (and also a huge benefit) when considering making a career in an international environment, which is my goal. 

Moreover, I specifically chose Toronto, Canada (as opposed to other Common law jurisdictions), because I have personal connection to the destination.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy to find the information that you needed to know. The office for exchange students and international students are very helpful, making sure that any and every question you have before and right on arrival are answered.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The student counsellor for exchange and international students at Osgoode invited exchange students over before semester start, so we could say hi, and I even got a quick tour of the Law School by one of the counsellors, as I was a winter exchange student and the introduction week for international students are held during the fall semester.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: For graduate/masters students, Osgoode Hall Law School / York University offers own apartments, studio apartments if you move alone, but 1 or 2 bedroom apartments are available for those, who move here with a partner, children or other immediate family members. It is either in Passy Garden, Assiboine or Atkinsons.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There were no meal plan options, but it didn't matter, as my apartment had its own kitchen (an actual kitchen and not just a kitchenette) and bathroom.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: For the semester of Winter 2023, the rent was 1,162 CAD, including heat, water and electricity. There is free wifi in the building (not always the strongest connection). The campus area is right next to the Law School, it takes no more than 5-8 minutes by foot, which is very convenient. The walls are thin, so you can hear your neighbors and people walk in the hallway, but I lived in Passy Garden, where most students are law students and therefore it was nice and quiet. Once a month they do a fire-alarm testing, so be prepared for that, but it takes no more than 15 minutes and it is always during work hours on week days. There are many take-away places in the nearby area, but the closest grocery store (i.e., Wal-mart, No frills etc. is a little further away - it is most convenient to take the bus or get a ride to these places, if you plan to buy for the week or so).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The wifi not working at random times was really a hassle, especially close to the exam period. However, the law library is always open, so you can always sit there and study. 

OBS! Be aware that you will only have the accommodation until the 30th of April at the latest as an exchange student. Thus, if you plan on staying for longer in Toronto, you have to make sure that you have a place to stay afterwards. Housing services won't even budge for an extra 1 or 2 weeks over stay, as the apartment is only rentable as long as you are enrolled as a student.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You will get an e-mail in July/August from Osgoode, which guides you through the course registration process, regardless of whether you are enrolled for the fall or winter term. You have to prioritize the courses you would like to take, and the courses are randomly assigned (no first-come first-serve basis). It is all done online and then you will get your courses by august. If you don't get the course you wanted, you can put yourself on a waitlist. In the first two weeks of every semester, you have the chance to change courses and drop out, and if you are waitlisted you might get accepted into a course you wanted in this time period. However, after the period is over you are locked with the courses you have chosen. Keep in mind that the classes proceed normally in this period, so if you change courses is up to you to catch up and eventually hand in assignments that have been due in this period of time.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Student Services and their counsellors are always there to help and guide you, including the exchange student coordinator, who works in the same place. They can all answer your questions. Moreover, there is an academic orientation for all new exchange students too, where any questions about courses and exams, student activities etc. were answered and explained.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was fairly successful. Out of my initial five courses that I wanted I got registered to my top three courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do not take more than one seminar course, unless you like to write a research paper at the same length as a bachelor thesis. I did not know this and took two seminar courses, and I had to write 2 x 30 pages papers.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses available to you as a masters student are upper year JD courses, meaning second and third year courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style of teaching depends on the course. In some classes, you will get participation mark and have to sign a sheet stating that you were in class. Therefore, the teaching and grading reminds me of the method used in Danish high school. To these classes it is important that you show up and participate actively. In seminar courses, it is usually the teachers talking, but you will have to do a little presentation in these courses as the grading is 80% your paper and 20% the presentation and/or participation. I also had hybrid classes, where some of it is online (zoom or audio lecture) and some in-person. It is common to show up and actively participate in class. 

Unlike UCPH, the grade is not based on one final exam (only in few courses - and even in these courses you can ask the professor, if you can write an optional paper, which weighs some of your marks). In most courses, the professors give you the option or require that you write an optional paper/do some assignments, so the exam is not 100 % of your mark. As opposed to UCPH, there are no oral examination - all in person examinations are usually between 2-3 hrs, otherwise you can get take-home examination, where the exam spans from 4 to 48 hrs depending on the course. In seminar courses, you will have to write research papers and submit before a specific date and time. 

Unlike UCPH, in most courses you are not required to buy books, as the professor hands you the material. In the few courses where a textbook was required, the professors claimed that not having the books will not make you fail, if you just studied the case law and the powerpoint slides.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Advanced Torts 
Taxation of Corporate Transactions
Trademarks
Legal Drafting 
Commercializing Intellectual Property

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would definitely recommend Legal Drafting, as it is such a practical course. You learn how to read and draft different types of contracts and the practical pitfalls, very interesting and definitely the best course, as it gives you so many tools on how to handle Canadian and American contracts. 

If you are interested in IP law, I would specifically recommend the Commercializing IP course. This course focus not only on the law, but also on the business and strategical aspects of IP, i.e., how businesses earn money by through IP, very interesting and also super practical. It is a seminar course, meaning you will have to write a paper or case study on a business using a IP strategy or a IP problem.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries are more expensive than I expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The primary student government is called "Legal&Lit", and it is responsible for coordinating and funding numerous professional, athletic, social and extracurricular activities at Osgoode Hall Law School. Make sure, you will get their weekly emails to your Osgoode email, so you don't miss out on all the fun activities they host. I can almost guarantee that there is something for anyone, as they really have branched out and have so many different clubs.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Legal&Lit hosts plenty of pub nights and social activities. It can be every thing from trivia nights, to panel debates, to ski trips and galas. I strongly recommend other exchange students to participate, as it will help you create a better network, and the other students are so nice and welcoming, so there is nothing to be afraid off. Some of the activities takes place at the JCR room (a hang out place at Law School) and others take place in downtown Toronto.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: The city of Toronto, Niagara Falls, if they have time and money, then definitely some of the other provinces in Canada or even the US.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy. People are so nice and welcoming, and they love small talk here.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just keep an open mind and attend classes, and you will make friends in no time. Canadian students are really friendly and super helpful. They naturally make sure that you are included in group work etc., if you tell them you are an exchange student and you instantly feel as if you have always known the local students. In most cases, regarding schoolwork, exams and even social activities, the best advice came from my peers. They are for sure better at giving you the ins and outs of how Law School works and how to have a good time. So, spend some time making friends in every class - as it can really be beneficial for you in the end.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None that I can think of. If you don't like small talk, then that can be a little challenging. Oh, and also remember to tip, when going to bars and restaurants! And, VAT is not included in the price, when you are shopping.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness of the people here and how multicultural this place is. You really meet a lot of interesting people.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Keep a positive attitude and an open mind - sometimes it can be daunting and hard to move to a whole new place on your own, but it will all work out for you with the right mindset. 
2. Try to make friends with other students - it can be really helpful, not only academically but also socially (which is just as important in order to thrive, because it can be hard to adjust and at times lonely moving to a new country. 
3. If you feel overwhelmed with the amount of courses and the work load, it is actually really normal. Even the local students feel the same pressure as you. In Denmark, we are used to 2-3 courses per semester, whereas it is quite normal to have 4-5 courses in Canada. But, do not get discouraged, just make sure you do everything in good time and then it is not so hard to juggle that many courses at once.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
You don't have that much time before semester ends and exams start (sometimes the last class and the first exam can be within one week), therefore do not wait until last minute to study for the exams or do your assignments. 

PLAN PLAN PLAN, make sure you have a solid plan in regard to where you will stay, your courses, what you want to see etc.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience is the fact that I now know that I can live alone and study in a foreign country. I have learned so many things not only academically but also on a personal level. There are so many things that I have gained from this trip, which I can use in order to enhance both my career and personal life.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being so far away from everything and anything you know, it takes some time to adjust and in the beginning it can feel a little lonely - no one really talks about this, but it is actually quite normal for exchange students. However, the feeling passes away quickly, provided you keep a positive attitude and an open mind :-).

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
